steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on the Incremental Fourier Neural Operator (iFNO): motivate FNO for solving PDEs, explain why choosing the number of Fourier modes and the training resolution matters, describe our incremental approach, and list our contributions.

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Deep learning for PDEs; FNO
  - DL solves PDEs much faster than traditional numerical methods in many domains
  - FNO: family of neural operators, state-of-the-art on PDEs
  - applications: turbulent flows, weather forecasting, material plasticity, carbon dioxide storage
  - learns solution operator: input (initial + boundary conditions) -> output (solution functions)
- How FNO works
  - discretization-convergence: predictions at different resolutions, converge to unique solution on mesh refinement
  - relies on kernel integration, realized with Fourier transform in FNO
  - spectral layers + normalization layers + non-linear activations = core architecture
  - many PDE systems (e.g. fluid flows): energy decays with frequency, low-freq components larger
  - frequency truncation T_{K} in each layer: only lowest K modes propagate, rest zeroed (Figure 1); inductive bias + regularization against overfitting
- The challenge
  - must pick right K in the spectral layers for good generalization
  - too few -> underfitting; too many -> overfitting
  - also need high-enough resolution data to capture all physical dynamics, approximate ground-truth operator
- Our approach: iFNO
  - incrementally + automatically increases modes K and resolution R during training
  - explained ratio = metric for how much of the spectrum current modes explain
  - below fixed threshold -> add more high-frequency modes (Figure 1)
  - start on low-res data, progressively increase resolution; like curriculum learning -> training efficiency
- Contributions
  - (1) iFNO: progressively increases spectral coefficients + data resolution; jointly or individually
  - (2) empirical validation: Burgers, Darcy Flow, Navier-Stokes, Kolmogorov Flow
  - (3) 10% lower test error (dynamical spectral regularization), 20% fewer modes vs FNO, 30% faster -> larger scale simulations

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Recently, deep learning has shown promise for solving partial differential equations (PDEs) much faster than traditional numerical methods, in many domains. One of these methods is the Fourier neural operator (FNO), proposed in earlier work, which is a family of neural operators that gets state-of-the-art performance in solving PDEs. It has been applied to modeling turbulent flows, weather forecasting, material plasticity, and carbon dioxide storage. FNO learns the solution operator of a PDE, which maps the input (initial and boundary conditions) to the output (solution functions).

FNO is different from conventional neural networks because it has a property called discretization-convergence. This means it can output predictions at different resolutions, and these predictions converge to a unique solution when the mesh is refined. The discretization-convergence property relies on kernel integration, and in FNO the kernel integration is done using the Fourier transform. A series of these spectral layers, together with normalization layers and non-linear activations, is the core of the FNO architecture. For many PDE systems, like fluid flows, the energy decays with frequency, which means low-frequency components usually have larger magnitudes than high-frequency ones. So FNO has a frequency truncation function T_{K} in each layer that only lets the lowest K Fourier modes go to the next layer and sets the other modes to zero, as shown in Figure 1. This works as an inductive bias and as a regularization to avoid overfitting.

So it is very important to choose the right number of frequency modes K in the different spectral layers of FNO to get the best generalization performance. If there are too few modes the model underfits, and if there are too many it can overfit. Also, we need to train on data with high enough resolution to capture all the physical dynamics and to approximate the ground-truth solution operator faithfully.

- Our approach: iFNO
  - incrementally + automatically increases modes K and resolution R during training
  - explained ratio = metric for how much of the spectrum current modes explain
  - below fixed threshold -> add more high-frequency modes (Figure 1)
  - start on low-res data, progressively increase resolution; like curriculum learning -> training efficiency
- Contributions
  - (1) iFNO: progressively increases spectral coefficients + data resolution; jointly or individually
  - (2) empirical validation: Burgers, Darcy Flow, Navier-Stokes, Kolmogorov Flow
  - (3) 10% lower test error (dynamical spectral regularization), 20% fewer modes vs FNO, 30% faster -> larger scale simulations

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Recently, deep learning has shown promise for solving partial differential equations (PDEs) much faster than traditional numerical methods, in many domains. One of these methods is the Fourier neural operator (FNO), proposed in earlier work, which is a family of neural operators that gets state-of-the-art performance in solving PDEs. It has been applied to modeling turbulent flows, weather forecasting, material plasticity, and carbon dioxide storage. FNO learns the solution operator of a PDE, which maps the input (initial and boundary conditions) to the output (solution functions).

FNO is different from conventional neural networks because it has a property called discretization-convergence. This means it can output predictions at different resolutions, and these predictions converge to a unique solution when the mesh is refined. The discretization-convergence property relies on kernel integration, and in FNO the kernel integration is done using the Fourier transform. A series of these spectral layers, together with normalization layers and non-linear activations, is the core of the FNO architecture. For many PDE systems, like fluid flows, the energy decays with frequency, which means low-frequency components usually have larger magnitudes than high-frequency ones. So FNO has a frequency truncation function T_{K} in each layer that only lets the lowest K Fourier modes go to the next layer and sets the other modes to zero, as shown in Figure 1. This works as an inductive bias and as a regularization to avoid overfitting.

So it is very important to choose the right number of frequency modes K in the different spectral layers of FNO to get the best generalization performance. If there are too few modes the model underfits, and if there are too many it can overfit. Also, we need to train on data with high enough resolution to capture all the physical dynamics and to approximate the ground-truth solution operator faithfully.

Our approach: We propose the Incremental Fourier neural operator (iFNO) to deal with these challenges. iFNO increases the number of frequency modes K and the resolution R incrementally and automatically during training. To increase the number of frequency modes dynamically, it uses the explained ratio as a metric. The explained ratio describes how much of the information in the underlying spectrum can be explained by the current set of modes. If the explained ratio is small (i.e., below a fixed threshold), the current modes are not enough to represent the target spectrum and more high-frequency modes should be added, as shown in Figure 1. At the same time, iFNO also starts by training on low-resolution data and then increases the resolution step by step, similar to the idea of curriculum learning, and this makes training more efficient.

Our contributions are the following:

1. We introduce the Incremental Fourier Neural Operator (iFNO), a new approach that progressively increases the number of spectral coefficients and the data resolution used during training. They can be used together or individually.

2. We do a thorough empirical validation on several partial differential equation (PDE) problems, including Burgers, Darcy Flow, the Navier-Stokes Equation, and the Kolmogorov Flow.

3. With iFNO, we show a 10% lower testing error, because it acts as a dynamical spectral regularization scheme, and it uses 20% fewer frequency modes than the existing Fourier Neural Operator, while also being 30% faster, which makes larger scale simulations possible.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Recently, deep learning has shown promise in solving partial differential equations (PDEs) significantly faster than traditional numerical methods in many domains. Among these methods, the Fourier neural operator (FNO), proposed by [1], is a family of neural operators that achieves state-of-the-art performance in solving PDEs, in applications modeling turbulent flows, weather forecasting [2], material plasticity [3], and carbon dioxide storage [4]. FNO learns the solution operator of a PDE that maps the input (initial and boundary conditions) to the output (solution functions).

Unlike conventional neural networks, FNO has a property called discretization-convergence: it can output predictions at different resolutions, and those predictions converge to a unique solution upon mesh refinement. This property relies on kernel integration, which FNO realizes using the Fourier transform. A series of such spectral layers, together with normalization layers and non-linear activations, forms the core of the FNO architecture. For many PDE systems, like fluid flows, energy decays with frequency, i.e., low-frequency components usually have larger magnitudes than high-frequency ones. Therefore, as an inductive bias and a regularization procedure to avoid overfitting, FNO has a frequency truncation function T_{K} in each layer that only allows the lowest K Fourier modes to propagate to the next layer, while the other modes are zeroed out, as shown in Figure 1.

It is thus crucial to select the right number of frequency modes K in the various spectral layers of FNO to achieve optimal generalization performance. Too few modes lead to underfitting, while too many can result in overfitting. Further, we need to train on data of high enough resolution to capture all the physical dynamics and faithfully approximate the ground-truth solution operator.

Our approach: We propose the Incremental Fourier neural operator (iFNO) to address these challenges. iFNO incrementally and automatically increases the number of frequency modes K and the resolution R during training. It uses the explained ratio as a metric to dynamically increase the number of frequency modes. The explained ratio characterizes how much of the information in the underlying spectrum the current set of modes can explain. A small explained ratio (i.e., below a fixed threshold) indicates that the current modes are insufficient to represent the target spectrum and that more high-frequency modes should be added, as illustrated in Figure 1. At the same time, iFNO also starts by training on low-resolution data and progressively increases the resolution, akin to curriculum learning, which increases training efficiency.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

1. We introduce the Incremental Fourier Neural Operator (iFNO), a novel approach that progressively increases the number of spectral coefficients and the data resolution used during training. These can be applied jointly or individually.

2. We perform a thorough empirical validation across a range of partial differential equation (PDE) problems, including Burgers, Darcy Flow, the Navier-Stokes Equation, and the Kolmogorov Flow.

3. Using iFNO, we demonstrate a 10% lower testing error by acting as a dynamical spectral regularization scheme, with 20% fewer frequency modes than the existing Fourier Neural Operator, while also being 30% faster, enabling larger scale simulations.

References:

Fourcastnet: A global data-driven high-resolution weather model using adaptive fourier neural operators. arXiv preprint arXiv:2202.11214 , 2022.
[3] Liu et al. (2022) Liu, B., Kovachki, N., Li, Z., Azizzadenesheli, K., Anandkumar, A., Stuart, A. M., and Bhattacharya, K. A learning-based multiscale method and its application to inelastic impact problems. Journal of the Mechanics and Physics of Solids , 158:104668, 2022.
